pages.title: US Asia-Pacific policy: alliances and containing China
pages.summary: Asia-Pacific is described as economically and strategically more important to the US than the Middle East, with US treaty allies and a policy of containing China since the Second World War. The page notes Mearsheimer's view that China's rise will not be peaceful, so containment must go with engagement, and that Obama's Asia Pivot is an old policy under a new name.

pages.title: Asia Rebalance and China's String of Pearls
pages.summary: Asia Pivot was renamed Asia Rebalance, with the Obama administration strengthening partnerships with Vietnam and India, normalising ties with Myanmar and deploying more US Marines, and India is called an ideal swing state. A US Defence Department report, 'Energy Futures in Asia', is cited for China's string of pearls, and ten Chinese pearls are listed from Hainan Island to Gwadar.

pages.title: Chinese and Indian views; India's own pearls
pages.summary: China says its ports protect trade and sea lines of communication from piracy, while India supports the US discourse and prioritises its navy with an aircraft carrier and nuclear submarines. The page lists India's pearls (Sittwe, Andaman and Nicobar command, Mauritius, Seychelles, Madagascar, Mozambique, Thumrait, Chabahar) and flags IORA for study.

pages.title: Indian naval diplomacy: Milan, Malabar, IONS, IORA
pages.summary: India pursues naval diplomacy through Milan exercises with South-East Asian navies, Malabar with the US and Japan, IBSAMAR and the Indian Ocean Naval Symposium. India, Australia and Mauritius are working to revive IORA, a 1990s organisation defunct until now, with a future goal of a free trade area.

pages.title: Act East, maritime doctrines, net security provider
pages.summary: Look East was primarily economic and focused on South-East Asia, whereas Act East is strategic and extends to the Asia-Pacific or Indo-Pacific. India's maritime doctrines are titled 'Freedom of Seas' (2009) and 'Ensuring Safe Seas' (2015), India sees itself as a net security provider, and the page begins the South China Sea stand with the 2015 India-US joint vision.

pages.title: India's South China Sea stand; sea's importance
pages.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs supports freedom of navigation, overflight and unimpeded commerce under UNCLOS, peaceful dispute resolution and self-restraint. India's interests include trade and investment growth since 1991 and oil and gas work with Vietnam, and the sea is a 1.4 mn sq. mile water body whose traffic is three times Suez and five times Panama.

pages.title: Strategic value of South China Sea; Kaplan's prediction
pages.summary: The sea is said to carry annual shipments of over $5 tn, likely holds oil and gas, and lies in the most densely populated region. Robert Kaplan's 2011 Foreign Policy article predicts it will be the future geopolitical hotspot, and the dispute is described as overlapping claims over the islands.

pages.title: China's assertiveness: artificial islands, motives, China Dream
pages.summary: China is laying claims to islands, building artificial islands that harm ecology, claiming the Senkaku and Diaoyu islands and setting up an Air Defence Identification Zone in the East China Sea, which the notes link to a slowing economy, party corruption and ultra-nationalism under the 'China Dream'. The page ends by introducing OBOR as the response to neighbours being pushed closer to adversaries.

pages.title: OBOR: Sareen's view and three objectives
pages.summary: Sushant Sareen calls OBOR neo-imperialism with Chinese characteristics, with geo-economic aims (forex reserves, infrastructure overcapacity, new markets, jobs), geo-political aims (soft power, a Sino-centric order, challenge to US hegemony) and geo-strategic aims (countering US containment by controlling choke points). OBOR also develops backward regions like Yunnan and has two dimensions: the 21st century Maritime Silk Road and the Silk Route Economic Belt.

pages.title: Six corridors of the Silk Route Economic Belt
pages.summary: The Silk Route Economic Belt has six sectors: China-Mongolia-Russia by the Trans-Siberian railways, the Eurasian land bridge, the China-Central Asia-West Asia corridor, the Indo-China Peninsula corridor, CPEC and the BCIM corridor. The page also reminds the student to prepare a map of OBOR.

pages.title: OBOR funding and India's reasons to stay out
pages.summary: About 60 countries are involved, funded by AIIB, China's EXIM Bank, a sovereign wealth fund and a Silk Route special fund. India will not join BCIM or CPEC because no government can compromise sovereignty, and the Foreign Secretary distinguishes multilateral AIIB, which India helped shape, from OBOR, a unilateral Chinese project announced in 2013.

pages.title: Debt concerns and alternatives to OBOR
pages.summary: The notes say OBOR is not good even for Pakistan, since countries unable to repay Chinese loans face land swaps, possibly over Gilgit-Baltistan. They advise India not to be a party to its own destruction, to work with like-minded countries and to see Japan's PQI as an alternative, adding that the BRICS summit shows India's bargaining power over South Asian neighbours.

flashcards.front: What was Obama's 'Asia Pivot' and how does it relate to US containment of China?
flashcards.back: The notes call it not a new policy but a new name for ongoing US policy, later renamed Asia Rebalance. It made peace and stability in Asia-Pacific a core US interest, strengthened partnerships with Vietnam and India, normalised ties with Myanmar and increased US Marines deployment.

flashcards.front: What is China's 'String of Pearls' and how does China respond to the charge?
flashcards.back: A US Defence Department report ('Energy Futures in Asia') says China is developing naval ports in the Indian Ocean, such as Hambantota, Gwadar and Djibouti, to contain India. China denies any containment policy and says the ports protect its trade and sea lines of communication from piracy.

flashcards.front: How is India responding to China's String of Pearls?
flashcards.back: India prioritises its navy (an aircraft carrier, nuclear submarines) and builds its own pearls such as Sittwe, the Andaman and Nicobar command, Mauritius, Seychelles, Chabahar and Thumrait. It also uses naval diplomacy through Milan, Malabar, IBSAMAR and IONS.

flashcards.front: How does Act East differ from Look East, and what is a 'net security provider'?
flashcards.back: Look East was primarily economic and focused on South-East Asia; Act East is strategic and extends to the Asia-Pacific or Indo-Pacific. A net security provider is a country that provides security to others too, against all threats, conventional and non-conventional.

flashcards.front: What is India's official stand on the South China Sea dispute?
flashcards.back: The MEA supports freedom of navigation, overflight and unimpeded commerce under UNCLOS, peaceful resolution without threat or use of force, and self-restraint. It calls the sea lines of communication critical to peace and stability and urges all parties to respect UNCLOS.

flashcards.front: What did Robert Kaplan predict about the South China Sea?
flashcards.back: In his 2011 Foreign Policy article, Kaplan predicted that the South China Sea will be the future geopolitical hotspot. He argued China will use it to erase centuries of foreign transgression and that it will determine the future of US power in Asia-Pacific.

flashcards.front: What are the geo-economic, geo-political and geo-strategic objectives of OBOR?
flashcards.back: Geo-economic: an outlet for forex reserves and infrastructure overcapacity, with diversified markets and jobs. Geo-political: soft power, a Sino-centric order and a challenge to US hegemony. Geo-strategic: countering US containment by controlling choke points.

flashcards.front: Why did India join AIIB but stay away from OBOR, according to the Foreign Secretary's distinction?
flashcards.back: AIIB is multilateral, India was involved since its conceptualisation, and it will not finance any project a member country objects to. OBOR is entirely a Chinese government project announced unilaterally in 2013 without consulting India, and CPEC and BCIM touch India's sovereignty.

answers.question: Why does the South China Sea matter to major powers? Examine China's assertiveness and India's interests and position on the dispute.
answers.intro: The South China Sea is a busy sea link where overlapping island claims meet Sino-US rivalry. China's assertiveness, shaped by domestic pressures, draws India in because of its trade and energy interests and its commitment to freedom of navigation.
body: Importance: a 1.4 mn sq. mile body stretching from the Singapore and Malacca straits to Taiwan, touching China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia, the Philippines and northern Indonesia. Its traffic is three times Suez and five times Panama, with over $5 tn of annual shipment and likely oil and gas.

Chinese posture: China lays claims to islands, builds ecologically harmful artificial islands, wants to turn the sea into a Chinese lake and foil US plans to choke its sea lines of communication. In the East China Sea it claims the Senkaku and Diaoyu islands and set up an Air Defence Identification Zone.

Motives: a slowing economy, party corruption and growing exposure to democracy lead China to raise ultra-nationalism through the 'China Dream'. Robert Kaplan predicted the sea would be the future hotspot.

India's position: the MEA backs freedom of navigation, overflight and commerce under UNCLOS, peaceful settlement and self-restraint. India's trade and investment have grown since 1991 and it plans oil and gas exploration with Vietnam; the 2015 India-US joint vision reflects this.
scholars: Robert D. Kaplan (Monsoon; 2011 Foreign Policy article)
answers.conclusion: India's stand pairs a principled call for UNCLOS-based peaceful settlement with real trade and energy interests. Naval capability and partnerships with Vietnam and the US will matter as the sea remains a geopolitical hotspot.

answers.question: Should India join China's One Belt One Road initiative? Critically examine.
answers.intro: OBOR is China's unilateral initiative linking Chinese cities with Europe through a maritime route and an economic belt. For India it offers connectivity but raises sovereignty, debt and strategic concerns, so the real choice is between joining and building alternatives.
body: China's objectives: geo-economic (outlet for forex reserves, use of infrastructure overcapacity, diversified markets), geo-political (soft power, a Sino-centric order, challenge to US hegemony) and geo-strategic (countering US containment by controlling choke points). Sushant Sareen calls it neo-imperialism with Chinese characteristics.

India's objections: India will not join BCIM or CPEC, as no government can compromise sovereignty and territorial integrity. OBOR was announced unilaterally at the 2013 ASEAN summit without consulting India, unlike AIIB, which India helped conceptualise and which cannot finance projects any member opposes.

Debt risk: countries joining are those unable to oppose China; loans carry heavy interest and unpaid debt leads to land swaps, so Pakistan may fall into debt and China may bargain for Gilgit-Baltistan. CPEC passes through Balochistan, and scholars say it is not good even for Pakistan.

Way forward: India should use resources wisely, work with like-minded countries and consider Japan's PQI as an alternative. China presses India because its inroads into South Asia are incomplete without it, and the BRICS summit shows India's bargaining power.
answers.conclusion: India is right to guard sovereignty and avoid debt dependence, but staying out is not a strategy by itself. Quality infrastructure partnerships such as Japan's PQI, and strong ties with neighbours, can offer connectivity without strategic cost.
